DENIZ AKKABAK · CHARACTER COMEDY TUTORIAL · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

MADE IN INVIDEO · invideo.io/i/DENIZ-ig

The Nose

One influencer, one very long nose, twenty small everyday disasters filmed like real phone footage, with sound. Built in invideo from Nano Banana Pro location plates, a character sheet and Seedance 2.5.

A TUTORIAL BY DENIZ AKKABAK · @DENIZ.AKKABAK

PIPELINE NANO BANANA PRO PLATES + CHARACTER SHEET → SEEDANCE 2.5 · 16:9 · 20 SCENES · 2:41 · AUDIO ON · BUILT IN INVIDEO

The Nose is a character series, and character comedy lives or dies on two things: the character must look exactly the same in every scene, and the world around him must feel completely real. The first version of this workflow put the man straight into every still, and it fought both goals at once. The version that works splits the job in two. Nano Banana Pro builds only the place: the street, the props, the extras, with an empty spot where he will stand. Seedance 2.5 then receives that plate as a location reference, never as a first frame, together with the character sheet, and stages the scene from its own angles.

The comedy is deliberately small. Nobody flies, nothing explodes. A mask sits on the nose and leaves the mouth uncovered; a bus door reopens because it touched his nose; the bar on a bench press stops halfway. Real behaviour of real objects, played straight, filmed by a stranger with a phone, with the room sound and a few lines of deadpan dialogue. Below is the full method, every plate, and every prompt exactly as it was run inside invideo.

THE PIPELINE AT A GLANCE

  1. 01

    Character sheet

    One turnaround sheet of the man (front, three-quarter, profile, back, face, hands, outfit) that goes into every video as @Image 2. It is the single source of truth for his face, nose, hair and clothes.

  2. 02

    Location plate — Nano Banana Pro

    One 16:9, 2K still per scene with everything except him: the place, the props, the supporting cast, and an empty spot where he will be. Shot as “a real photo shot on an iPhone”.

  3. 03

    Video — Seedance 2.5, audio on

    The plate goes in as @Image 1, labelled as location only, plus the sheet as @Image 2. Ten seconds, 1080p, two to five shots with hard cuts, ambient sound, sound effects and short dialogue, never music.

STEP 01 — THE CHARACTER

One Sheet, Every Scene

Everything starts from the character sheet below. Every video prompt points at it as @Image 2 and limits its job precisely: use only his face, long nose, curly hair, mustache, build and outfit, and ignore the grid, the labels and the grey studio background. Without that last clause, models happily copy the sheet’s studio backdrop or its panel layout into the scene. The consistency line repeats the most important rule in plain words: his nose keeps the same size and shape.

STEP 02 — SETTING UP IN INVIDEO

Plates First, Then Performance

  1. 01

    Nano Banana Pro

    Aspect ratio 16:9, resolution 2K. Prompt field for the plate description, separate negative field that bans the main character himself, camera interfaces, studio light and the cinematic look.

  2. 02

    Seedance 2.5 (reference to video)

    Attach the plate first so it becomes @Image 1, the character sheet second so it becomes @Image 2, and any product third (@Image 3, the Kith tee in the opening scene). Duration 10 seconds, resolution 1080p, audio generation on.

  3. 03

    Timeline

    All clips on one invideo timeline; each take trimmed to the window where the moment reads cleanly.

STEP 03 — THE METHOD

Location, Not First Frame

The single most important sentence in every video prompt is “@Image 1 = location reference only, not a start frame: the same place, filmed from its own angle.” If a plate is used as a first frame, the video is trapped in that exact composition and the character has to appear out of nowhere inside it. Used as a location reference, the plate gives Seedance the street, the light, the props and the extras, and Seedance is free to cut between angles, which is how these clips get a wide shot from across the road and then a closer shot of the moment.

Two other rules came from revisions. First, restraint: early prompts were too big, with ice cream scoops stuck to the nose and doors trapping him. The final prompts describe the smallest believable version of each accident and add “no exaggerated cartoon acting” to every negative list. Second, sound: every clip is generated with audio on, with the room tone, the specific sound effects and any dialogue written into an AUDIO line, lines of dialogue in curly braces, a fixed VOICE description for the man, and “No music” in every prompt, so the edit can add its own track.

STEP 04

Anatomy — Why These Prompts Work

  1. 01

    Location, not first frame

    “@Image 1 = location reference only, not a start frame.” The plate supplies the world; Seedance chooses the angles. This is what allows real coverage: a wide from across the street, then a closer shot of the moment.

  2. 02

    The sheet, limited

    “Use only his face, long nose, curly hair, mustache, build and outfit; ignore the grid, labels and grey background.” A character sheet is a powerful reference, but only if you tell the model which parts of it to ignore.

  3. 03

    Shots with hard cuts

    “Two shots with one hard cut”, then SHOT 1 and SHOT 2 with timestamps. Writing the cut into the prompt turns a single generation into edited coverage; the pharmacy scene pushes it to five angles in ten seconds.

  4. 04

    The stranger’s phone

    “A bystander’s phone, handheld, natural shake, one or two short digital zooms, focus briefly drifting.” The camera never belongs to a film crew, which is why the footage reads as something that really happened.

  5. 05

    Restraint

    Every accident is the smallest believable version: a dab of ice cream, a door sensor, a half rep. “No exaggerated cartoon acting” in every negative list keeps performances human.

  6. 06

    The sound layer

    An AUDIO line with room tone and specific effects, dialogue in curly braces, a fixed VOICE line for the man, and “No music” in every prompt. Sound is half of the realism, and keeping music out keeps the edit flexible.

  7. 07

    The insurance

    The plate negatives ban the main character himself, so Nano Banana Pro never sneaks him into a plate; the video negatives ban opening on the plate as a frozen still, the sheet’s grid and labels, camera interfaces and morphing.

THE RESULT

Output — The Nose

Check your own cut against three things. Does the man look identical in every scene? Is every accident small enough to be believable? Can you hear the place? And does the camera feel like a stranger who happened to be there? If all four hold, the character carries the series.

ONE CHARACTER · TWENTY PLACES · ZERO MUSIC

The world is real. Only the nose is not.

Swap the nose for any defining trait, giant hair, extreme height, a voice that is far too loud, and the skeleton carries any character: one turnaround sheet, empty location plates, a location-not-first-frame reference, small real-world accidents written as shots with hard cuts, and a sound layer with no music.
